mainTopic: Handling תפילין: holding them in a בית הכסא, at a meal, with money, and while sleeping
overview: This amud opens with stories of רבי יוחנן and רב נחמן, who kept their תפילין in hand because they would protect them. A ברייתא forbids praying, urinating, or sleeping while holding תפילין, and שמואל adds that ordinary objects also distract from prayer. רב ששת claims this ברייתא follows only בית שמאי. After a long back-and-forth about uncovering טפחים, the גמרא concludes that בית הלל also forbid holding תפילין in a makeshift בית הכסא, so רב ששת is refuted. The reason is splashing drops, a practical reason that stands outside the קל וחומר. The גמרא then teaches how to prepare for a סעודת קבע and what to do with one's תפילין at the meal. Next it discusses whether תפילין may be bundled with money in a cloth, which depends on designation, with רב חסדא and אביי disagreeing. Finally, שמואל permits placing תפילין under one's head even with his wife present. A ברייתא refutes him, yet רבא rules like him, and the reason for this ruling comes on the next amud.

steps.title: רב נחמן kept his תפילין in hand for protection
steps.stepSummary: The previous story ends with 'they will protect me.' רבא then reports that רב נחמן let his students carry his book of אגדתא but kept his תפילין himself, because the רבנן permitted holding them and they would protect him.
steps.simpleTranslation: …they will protect me. רבא said: When we walked behind רב נחמן, if he was holding a book of אגדתא, he would give it to us to carry. If he was holding תפילין, he would not give them to us. He said: Since the רבנן permitted holding them, they will protect me.
steps.whatsHappening: The first word, נִינְטְרַן, ends the previous story about רבי יוחנן. רבא then tells a second story showing that רב נחמן also kept his תפילין in his own hands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The contrast is the point: a regular holy book could be handed to a student, but תפילין were kept. רב נחמן's reason is that since the רבנן allowed a person to hold תפילין, holding them gives the person a שמירה (protection). This supports the practice described in the story just before it.

keyTerms.meaning: A book of אגדה (non-legal Torah teachings)

steps.confusionAlert: The first word נִינְטְרַן is not part of רבא's story. It is the last word of the previous story about רבי יוחנן. The same word appears again at the end of רב נחמן's statement.

phrases.english: they will protect me.
phrases.notes: Ending of the previous story about רבי יוחנן holding his תפילין

phrases.english: Rava said:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֲוָה אָזְלִינַן בָּתְרֵיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן,
phrases.english: When we would walk after Rav Nachman,
when he was holding a book of aggada,
he would give it to us;
when he was holding tefillin,
he would not give them to us.
He said: Since the Rabbis permitted them,
they will protect me.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: כִּי הֲוָה אָזְלִינַן בָּתְרֵיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallels the preceding story (earlier) about רבי יוחנן keeping his tefillin in hand for protection
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Since holding תפילין is permitted, one may keep them in hand, and they provide protection; a regular holy book may be handed to others.

steps.title: A ברייתא: do not pray, urinate, or sleep while holding תפילין
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches three things. One may not pray while holding תפילין or a ספר תורה. One may not urinate while holding them. One may not sleep while holding them, whether a real sleep or a short nap.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: A person should not hold תפילין in his hand or a ספר תורה in his arm and pray. He should not urinate while holding them. He should not sleep while holding them, neither a full sleep nor a short nap.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that lists situations in which a person may not be holding holy objects.
steps.deeperAnalysis: While praying, the worry that the object might fall distracts him from his prayer. Urinating or sleeping while holding holy objects is improper and risks disrespect to them. This ברייתא sets up רב ששת's ruling later, which focuses on the urination rule.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A person may not hold tefillin in his hand
or a Torah scroll in his arm and pray.
And he may not urinate with them,
and he may not sleep with them,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שֵׁינַת קֶבַע וְלֹא שֵׁינַת עֲרַאי.
phrases.english: neither a fixed sleep nor a casual nap.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: לֹא יֹאחַז אָדָם תְּפִילִּין בְּיָדוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After stories that permit holding תפילין, the גמרא brings a source that limits when one may hold them
steps.mimraCoreRuling: While holding תפילין or a ספר תורה, one may not pray, urinate, or sleep (fixed or casual).

steps.title: שמואל: holding ordinary objects also disturbs prayer
steps.stepSummary: שמואל adds that holding a knife, money, a bowl, or a loaf of bread is the same: one should not pray while holding them.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: A knife, money, a bowl, and a loaf of bread are in the same category as these.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל extends the first rule of the ברייתא, about prayer, to ordinary objects.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His addition shows that the prayer rule is about distraction, not only about the holiness of the object. Anything a person worries might fall or get ruined will take his mind off his תפילה.

keyTerms.meaning: Like them, in the same category

phrases.english: Shmuel said:
A knife, money, a bowl, and a loaf of bread —
these are like them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: סַכִּין וּמָעוֹת וּקְעָרָה וְכִכָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands the prayer rule of the ברייתא to everyday objects
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may not pray while holding a knife, money, a bowl, or bread, because they distract him just as holy objects do.

steps.title: רב ששת: the ברייתא follows בית שמאי, so it is not the הלכה
steps.stepSummary: רבא quotes רב ששת: the הלכה does not follow this ברייתא, because it follows בית שמאי. בית הלל allow holding תפילין in a permanent בית הכסא, so they would certainly allow it in the lesser case of a makeshift one, such as simply urinating.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said in the name of רב ששת: The הלכה is not like this ברייתא, because it follows בית שמאי. If it followed בית הלל, consider this: they permit holding תפילין in a permanent בית הכסא. Do we even need to say that a makeshift בית הכסא is permitted?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת rejects the ruling of the ברייתא that one may not urinate while holding תפילין, and he proves it must be the view of בית שמאי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier in the sugya, בית הלל allowed a person to hold his תפילין in his hand while entering a permanent בית הכסא. That is the stricter case, so the easier case, urinating in a makeshift spot, must be allowed even more (a קל וחומר). Since the ברייתא forbids the easier case, it cannot follow בית הלל, and we do not rule like בית שמאי against בית הלל.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא (here, the teaching just quoted)
A makeshift, temporary bathroom (for example, urinating outdoors)
Is it necessary to say? (implies: obviously)

steps.confusionAlert: Here מַתְנִיתָא does not mean the משנה. It refers to the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.whyThisMatters: According to רב ששת, the practical הלכה follows בית הלל, so one may hold תפילין while urinating. But this claim is challenged in step 5 and conclusively refuted (תיובתא) in step 12.

phrases.english: Rava said that Rav Sheshet said:
The halacha is not in accordance with this baraita,
because it is the view of Beit Shammai.
For if it were Beit Hillel —
now, in a permanent bathroom they permit it;
is it even necessary to say that a makeshift bathroom is permitted?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: לֵית הִלְכְתָא כִּי הָא מַתְנִיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the urination rule of the ברייתא in step 2 by identifying its author as בית שמאי
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הלכה does not follow the ברייתא's ban on urinating while holding תפילין, because the ban follows בית שמאי; בית הלל permit it.

steps.title: Challenge: 'What I permitted here, I forbade there' fits only בית הלל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב ששת with the phrase 'things I permitted you here, I forbade you there,' which seems to refer to תפילין. That phrase works for בית הלל: permitted in a permanent בית הכסא, forbidden in a makeshift one. According to בית שמאי, nothing was permitted at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: They objected: 'Things I permitted you here, I forbade you there.' Isn't this talking about תפילין? It makes sense if you say this follows בית הלל: I permitted you here, in a permanent בית הכסא, and I forbade you there, in a makeshift בית הכסא. But if you say it follows בית שמאי, they did not permit anything at all!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב ששת's claim that the urination ban follows בית שמאי, using a teaching that seems to show בית הלל also forbid holding תפילין in a makeshift בית הכסא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase describes something allowed in one place and forbidden in another. Under בית הלל this fits well: allowed in a permanent בית הכסא but forbidden in a makeshift one, which matches the ברייתא's ban on urinating with תפילין. Under בית שמאי, nothing was ever allowed with תפילין in a בית הכסא, so 'what I permitted you' would be meaningless. That suggests the ban comes from בית הלל, against רב ששת.

keyTerms.meaning: They raised an objection (from a תנאי source)
Is it not? (proposes an interpretation as the basis of a challenge)
It is understandable (according to one view)

steps.confusionAlert: It seems strange that a permanent בית הכסא would be more lenient than a makeshift one. The 'permitted here' refers to the permanent one, and the 'forbidden there' refers to the makeshift one. The גמרא raises this oddity directly in step 13 and explains it (splashing drops) in step 14.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
Matters which I permitted you here,
I forbade you there.
What, is it not referring to tefillin?
Granted, if you say it follows Beit Hillel:
I permitted you here — in a permanent bathroom;

phrases.aramaic: אָסַרְתִּי לְךָ כָּאן בֵּית הַכִּסֵּא עֲרַאי.
phrases.english: I forbade you there — in a makeshift bathroom.
But if you say it follows Beit Shammai,
they did not permit anything at all!

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: דְּבָרִים שֶׁהִתַּרְתִּי לְךָ כָּאן, אָסַרְתִּי לְךָ כָּאן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב ששת's claim in step 4 that the ban on urinating with תפילין follows בית שמאי
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's claim that the ברייתא's ban on urinating while holding תפילין follows בית שמאי and is not the halacha
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The phrase 'what I permitted here, I forbade there' implies something permitted in a permanent בית הכסא but forbidden in a makeshift one. Only בית הלל permitted anything, namely holding תפילין in a permanent בית הכסא. So the ban in a makeshift בית הכסא must also be בית הלל's view.

steps.title: The phrase is not about תפילין but about uncovering one or two handbreadths
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא defends רב ששת. It says the phrase 'permitted here, forbidden there' was taught about how many טפחים to uncover, not about תפילין.
steps.simpleTranslation: When that ברייתא was taught, it was talking about one טפח and two טפחים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 5. The phrase 'permitted here, forbidden there' was never about holding תפילין. It was about how much of the body a person may uncover.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge only worked if the phrase was about תפילין. Moving the phrase to a different topic means it no longer proves anything about holding תפילין in the בית הכסא. So רב ששת's claim survives: the strict ברייתא follows בית שמאי.

keyTerms.meaning: When that [ברייתא] was taught. It introduces a new reading of a source.
With regard to, about the topic of

phrases.english: When that [teaching] was taught,
phrases.notes: Refers to the phrase 'things I permitted you here, I forbade you there' from step 5.

phrases.english: it was about one handbreadth and two handbreadths.
phrases.notes: In other words, about how much of the body to uncover, not about תפילין.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי תַּנְיָא הַהִיא, לְעִנְיַן טֶפַח וְטִפְחַיִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 5 by moving the challenging phrase to a different topic.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the source's subject matter
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrase 'permitted here, forbidden there' was about holding תפילין, which would contradict רב ששת.
steps.terutzMaskana: The phrase is about how many טפחים one may uncover, so it says nothing about תפילין.
steps.whyThisMatters: This saves רב ששת's position that the strict ברייתא about holding תפילין while urinating follows בית שמאי.

steps.title: Two ברייתות disagree on how much to uncover in front
steps.stepSummary: Both ברייתות allow one טפח behind. One allows two טפחים in front, and the other allows nothing in front.
steps.simpleTranslation: One ברייתא teaches: when a person relieves himself, he uncovers one טפח behind and two טפחים in front. Another ברייתא teaches: one טפח behind and nothing at all in front.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the two sources that the phrase is really about. They seem to contradict each other, and this sets up the next move: explaining how both can be true.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sources agree about the back: one טפח. They disagree about the front: two טפחים or none. 'Permitted here, forbidden there' will turn out to mean that uncovering the front is allowed in one case and forbidden in another.

phrases.english: As one [ברייתא] teaches:
When he relieves himself,
he uncovers one handbreadth behind him
and two handbreadths in front of him.
And another [ברייתא] teaches:
one handbreadth behind him
and in front of him, nothing at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתָנֵי חֲדָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the actual sources that step 6 said the phrase refers to.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both sources allow one טפח behind. In front, one source allows two טפחים and the other allows none.

steps.title: Suggestion: one source is about the big need, the other about urinating
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that both sources are about a man. The 'nothing in front' source is about the big need, and the 'two טפחים' source is about urinating.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't it that both are talking about a man, and there is no contradiction? Here it is about the big need, and there it is about the small need.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a way to make the two ברייתות fit together. That would also explain the phrase 'permitted here, forbidden there.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The suggestion has two parts. When urinating, a man may uncover two טפחים in front. For the big need he may uncover nothing in front. So uncovering in front is 'permitted here' (urinating) and 'forbidden there' (the big need), which fits the phrase neatly.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it not that…? This introduces a suggested explanation.
This one and that one, meaning both sources
And it is not difficult; there is no contradiction

steps.confusionAlert: Here גדולים and קטנים do NOT mean adults and children. They are polite words for the two kinds of bathroom needs.

phrases.english: Is it not that both this one and that one are about a man,
and there is no contradiction:
here it is for the big need, there it is for the small need?
phrases.notes: Big need means nothing uncovered in front. Small need means two handbreadths in front.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי לָאו אִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי בְּאִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction between the two ברייתות of step 7 and ties it to the phrase from step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא) by type of need
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: One ברייתא is about the big need and the other about urinating, which matches 'permitted here, forbidden there.'

steps.title: Rejection: urinating would not require uncovering behind
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. If one source were about urinating, why would it require uncovering one טפח behind?
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you really think so? If it is about urinating, why do I need one טפח behind?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the suggestion from step 8.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'two טפחים in front' ברייתא also mentions one טפח behind. Uncovering behind makes no sense for urinating. So that ברייתא cannot be about urinating, and the split between the big and small need falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: And can you really think that? This introduces a rejection.

phrases.english: And can you really think so?!
If it is about the small need (urinating),
why do I need one handbreadth behind him?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתִסְבְּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the resolution offered in step 8.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The full suggestion that one ברייתא is about urinating
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא requires one טפח behind, which only makes sense for the big need, not for urinating.

steps.title: New answer: both are about the big need, one for a man and one for a woman
steps.stepSummary: Both ברייתות are about the big need. The 'two טפחים in front' source is about a man, and the 'nothing in front' source is about a woman.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, both are about the big need, and there is no contradiction. This one is about a man, and that one is about a woman.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the first suggestion failed, the גמרא offers a different way to reconcile the two ברייתות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A man may need to uncover two טפחים in front in case he urinates at the same time. A woman does not need to uncover anything in front. The difference now depends on who the person is, not on which need it is.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. It introduces a replacement answer.

phrases.english: Rather, both this one and that one are about the big need,
and there is no contradiction:
this one is about a man, that one is about a woman.
phrases.notes: A man uncovers two handbreadths in front in case he urinates. A woman uncovers nothing in front.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי בִּגְדוֹלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected answer of step 8 with a new split: man versus woman.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא) by the person involved
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות are split by the big need versus urinating.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both are about the big need. The difference is a man versus a woman.

steps.title: Challenge: a man-woman difference is not a surprising קל וחומר
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא calls its ruling 'a קל וחומר that has no answer.' A simple man-woman difference is just natural, so why describe it that way?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the ברייתא adds: 'This is a קל וחומר that has no answer.' What does 'has no answer' mean? That is simply the way things are!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the man-woman answer from step 10, using the extra words the ברייתא says about this ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא presents its ruling as something that goes against what logic would expect. That fits a case where something is allowed in the stricter-seeming situation (a permanent בית הכסא) yet forbidden in the lighter one (a makeshift בית הכסא), since a קל וחומר would say the lighter case is surely allowed. A difference between a man and a woman goes against nothing; it is just how bodies are built. So the ברייתא's words do not fit the step 10 answer.

keyTerms.meaning: If so. It introduces a challenge to the last answer.
That is taught about it, an extra line attached to the ruling
A קל וחומר that has no answer: a ruling that surprisingly goes against expected logic
The natural way of the matter

steps.whatToRemember: The phrase is not about תפילין but about how many טפחים to uncover. 'Big need versus small need' was rejected. 'Man versus woman' is now under attack, because the ברייתא's 'קל וחומר with no answer' wording points to a surprising ruling, not a natural difference.

phrases.english: If so,
that which is taught about it,
'This is an a fortiori argument that has no answer' —
what does 'has no answer' mean?
That is simply the natural way things are!
phrases.notes: Men and women naturally need to uncover differently. There is nothing surprising here.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי הָא דְּקָתָנֵי עֲלַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the man-woman answer of step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the two ברייתות are about a man and a woman
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא calls its ruling a surprising 'קל וחומר with no answer.' A natural man-woman difference is not surprising, so the wording does not fit that answer.

steps.title: The ברייתא must be about תפילין, so רבא's reading is refuted
steps.stepSummary: Since the 'uncovering' explanations failed, the ברייתא must be about holding תפילין. The reading of רבא in the name of רב ששת is conclusively refuted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, isn't it about תפילין? And this is a refutation of what רבא said in the name of רב ששת. Yes, it is a refutation.
steps.whatsHappening: Every attempt to read the ברייתא as being about uncovering טפחים has failed. So the גמרא concludes that the ברייתא is really about holding תפילין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 8-11 tried to fit 'what I permitted you here, I forbade you there' to the rules about uncovering, and none of those attempts held up. So it refers to תפילין: permitted in a בית הכסא קבוע and forbidden in a בית הכסא עראי. Only בית הלל permit anything in a בית הכסא קבוע, so בית הלל themselves forbid holding תפילין while urinating. That refutes רב ששת's claim that the strict ברייתא is only בית שמאי's view.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Rather, is it not...?' This introduces the only option still left.
A conclusive refutation of an Amora's statement

steps.whatToRemember: The 'uncovering' reading is finished. From here on, the ברייתא is understood as being about holding תפילין in a bathroom.
steps.confusionAlert: The word תיובתא appears twice. The first time it raises the refutation. The second, standalone תיובתא is the גמרא confirming it: 'Yes, it is refuted.'

phrases.english: Rather, is it not about tefillin?
And this is a refutation of Rava, who said in the name of Rav Sheshet.
It is indeed a refutation.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לָאו, תְּפִילִּין, וּתְיוּבְתָּא דְרָבָא אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 11's question knocks out the last 'uncovering' reading. This step draws the conclusion from that.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ברייתא is about תפילין, and רבא's statement in the name of רב ששת is refuted.

steps.title: The logic seems backwards: a makeshift bathroom should be easier
steps.stepSummary: Even with the ברייתא about תפילין, its ruling is hard to understand. If תפילין are allowed in a permanent bathroom, they should surely be allowed in a temporary one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Either way, it is difficult. Now, if a regular bathroom is permitted, isn't a makeshift bathroom all the more so?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts that the ברייתא is about תפילין. But now it questions the ruling itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא allows holding תפילין in a בית הכסא קבוע but forbids it in a בית הכסא עראי. Normally a permanent bathroom is the more serious place. So the קל וחומר should lead to the opposite result: if the more serious place is allowed, the lighter place should certainly be allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: A permanent, regular bathroom (one sits there)
A makeshift, temporary bathroom (for urinating while standing)
Not all the more so? This is the language of a קל וחומר.

phrases.english: Either way, it is difficult:
Now, if a regular bathroom is permitted,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּית הַכִּסֵּא עֲרַאי לֹא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן!
phrases.english: a makeshift bathroom, all the more so!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִכׇּל מָקוֹם, קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The reading is now settled as being about תפילין, so the גמרא turns to the logic of the ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's rule that תפילין are allowed in a בית הכסא קבוע but forbidden in a בית הכסא עראי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A קל וחומר from the stricter place to the lighter place should permit תפילין in the makeshift bathroom, not forbid them.

steps.title: The difference is the splashing drops
steps.stepSummary: In a regular bathroom one sits, so there are no drops. In a makeshift bathroom one stands and urine splashes, so holding תפילין is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it means: in a regular bathroom, where there are no drops, they permitted it. In a makeshift bathroom, where there are drops, they forbade it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the rule is not about how serious each place is. It is about a practical problem: splashing drops.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a makeshift bathroom, drops of urine splash onto a person's clothes. He may then wipe them with the same hand that is holding the תפילין. In a regular bathroom there are no such drops, so this danger does not exist. That practical difference explains why the stricter-sounding place is actually the one that is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: 'This is what it means.' This introduces a clarifying explanation.

phrases.english: This is what it means:
a regular bathroom, where there are no drops,
they permitted.
a makeshift bathroom, where there are drops,
they forbade.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 13's קשיא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Introduces a practical, factual reason that overrides the expected קל וחומר
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We assumed the rule depended on how serious each bathroom is.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule depends on whether there are splashing drops, which could lead one to touch them with the hand holding the תפילין.

steps.title: If there is a clear reason, why say 'it has no answer'?
steps.stepSummary: If the splashing drops explain the difference, that is an excellent answer. So why does the ברייתא call it a קל וחומר שאין עליו תשובה?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why does it say 'there is no answer to it'? This is an excellent answer!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks its own explanation. A clear practical reason seems to contradict the ברייתא's wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא describes its ruling as a קל וחומר that cannot be answered. But the splashing drops are exactly the kind of refutation that would break a קל וחומר. So the explanation from step 14 seems to clash with the ברייתא's own language.

keyTerms.meaning: 'If so.' This introduces a challenge built on the previous answer.

steps.confusionAlert: Here תשובה does not mean 'repentance'. It means a refutation or counter-argument against the קל וחומר.

phrases.english: If so,
why does it say 'there is no answer to it'?
It is an excellent answer!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אַמַּאי ״אֵין עָלָיו תְּשׁוּבָה״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's phrase 'אין עליו תשובה' as it fits with the explanation in step 14
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The splashing-drops distinction is itself a strong refutation, so the קל וחומר cannot be described as having no answer.

steps.title: Use the practical reason, not the inference
steps.stepSummary: The different bathroom rulings come from their different circumstances, not from a קַל וָחוֹמֶר.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it means: Derive this matter from its reason, not by a קַל וָחוֹמֶר. If you try to derive it by a קַל וָחוֹמֶר, that would be a קַל וָחוֹמֶר with no answer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גְּמָרָא answers the previous challenge by explaining how to read the source’s wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sitting in a regular bathroom avoids splashing; standing in a makeshift one does not. That practical difference explains the ruling. The source calls the קַל וָחוֹמֶר unanswerable because the practical explanation is not a rebuttal to the inference itself.

keyTerms.meaning: On the basis of a reason.
By an inference from the less strict case to the stricter one.

steps.whatToRemember: The ruling has a practical reason; it is not being derived by a קַל וָחוֹמֶר.

phrases.aramaic: הָכִי קָאָמַר: הָא מִילְּתָא תֵּיתֵי לַהּ בְּתוֹרַת טַעְמָא,
phrases.english: This is what it means: Derive this matter on the basis of its reason,
and do not derive it by an inference from the less strict case to the stricter one,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִי אָתְיָא לַהּ בְּתוֹרַת קַל וָחוֹמֶר,
phrases.english: because if you derive it through that kind of inference,

phrases.aramaic: זֶהוּ קַל וָחוֹמֶר שֶׁאֵין עָלָיו תְּשׁוּבָה.
phrases.english: that is an inference to which there is no rebuttal.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי קָאָמַר: הָא מִילְּתָא תֵּיתֵי לַהּ בְּתוֹרַת טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 15’s challenge to the wording of the earlier source.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes an explanation based on circumstances from a formal inference.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The explanation about splashing seemed to be an answer to the קַל וָחוֹמֶר.
steps.terutzMaskana: The explanation gives the ruling’s practical reason; the קַל וָחוֹמֶר itself is not the way to derive the ruling.

steps.title: Prepare before sitting down to a regular meal
steps.stepSummary: A person about to enter a סְעוּדַת קֶבַע should walk a specified amount, relieve himself, and only then enter.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: Someone who wants to enter a regular meal walks four cubits ten times, or ten cubits four times, relieves himself, and then enters.
steps.whatsHappening: The גְּמָרָא moves from the bathroom discussion to a new teaching about preparing for a regular meal. This sets up the next discussion of תְּפִילִּין at that meal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both walking patterns total forty cubits. The person takes care of bodily needs before beginning the meal.

phrases.aramaic: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הָרוֹצֶה לִיכָּנֵס לִסְעוּדַת קֶבַע,
phrases.english: The Sages taught: One who wants to enter a regular meal
walks four cubits ten times,
or ten cubits four times,
relieves himself, and then enters.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הָרוֹצֶה לִיכָּנֵס לִסְעוּדַת קֶבַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new teaching after the prior challenge is resolved.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Walk the stated distance and relieve oneself before entering a סְעוּדַת קֶבַע.

steps.title: Remove the תפילין before entering the meal
steps.stepSummary: רַבִּי יִצְחָק says to remove תְּפִילִּין before entering a סְעוּדַת קֶבַע.
steps.simpleTranslation: רַבִּי יִצְחָק said: One who enters a regular meal removes his תְּפִילִּין and then enters.
steps.whatsHappening: The גְּמָרָא adds another instruction about entering a סְעוּדַת קֶבַע, now concerning תְּפִילִּין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The order matters: remove the תְּפִילִּין first, then enter the meal. The next statement will give a different instruction about where to put them.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: הַנִּכְנָס לִסְעוּדַת קֶבַע,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzḥak said: One who enters a regular meal
removes his tefillin and then enters.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: הַנִּכְנָס לִסְעוּדַת קֶבַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second preparation for the same kind of meal.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Remove תְּפִילִּין before entering a סְעוּדַת קֶבַע.

steps.title: Place the תפילין on the table
steps.stepSummary: The גְּמָרָא presents רַבִּי חִיָּיא as disagreeing: he says to place the תְּפִילִּין on the table.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this disagrees with רַבִּי חִיָּיא, who said: He places them on his table, and doing so is fitting for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גְּמָרָא explicitly introduces a differing view about what to do with the תְּפִילִּין at the meal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רַבִּי יִצְחָק told the person to remove them before entering. רַבִּי חִיָּיא instead describes placing them on the table and calls that fitting.

keyTerms.meaning: The sage whose differing view follows.

phrases.aramaic: וּפְלִיגָא דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא:
phrases.english: And it disagrees with Rabbi Ḥiyya, for Rabbi Ḥiyya said:

phrases.aramaic: מַנִּיחָן עַל שֻׁלְחָנוֹ, וְכֵן הָדוּר לוֹ.
phrases.english: He places them on his table, and that is fitting for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּפְלִיגָא דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces an explicitly differing instruction about the תְּפִילִּין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Place the תְּפִילִּין on the table during the meal; doing so is fitting.

steps.title: The arrangement lasts until the blessing
steps.stepSummary: A brief question asks how long the meal-time arrangement lasts; רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק answers: until the time of the blessing.
steps.simpleTranslation: And until when? רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק said: Until the time of the blessing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גְּמָרָא asks for the endpoint of the meal-time practice and immediately supplies an answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier statements described what happens to תְּפִילִּין at a regular meal, but did not give an endpoint. רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק sets that endpoint at the time of the blessing after the meal.

keyTerms.meaning: The sage who gives the endpoint.

steps.whatToRemember: The stated endpoint is זְמַן בְּרָכָה.

phrases.english: And until when?
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said:
Until the time of the blessing.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעַד אֵימַת? אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies how long the meal-time instruction about תְּפִילִּין applies.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Until the time of the blessing after the meal.

steps.title: Two teachings give opposite rules
steps.stepSummary: One teaching permits bundling תְּפִילִּין with money; another forbids it.
steps.simpleTranslation: One teaching says a person may bundle his תְּפִילִּין with his money in his head covering. Another says he may not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גְּמָרָא puts two conflicting teachings side by side. It is setting up a need to explain why they differ.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both teachings discuss keeping תְּפִילִּין and money together. One permits it and the other forbids it, so some difference between their cases must be found.

phrases.english: One teaching taught: A person may bundle his phylacteries
with his money in his head covering.
But another teaching taught: He may not bundle them.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנֵי חֲדָא: צוֹרֵר אָדָם תְּפִילָּיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the meal-time handling of תְּפִילִּין to a new question about their covering.
steps.kashyaTarget: The permission to bundle תְּפִילִּין with money.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A second teaching explicitly says not to bundle them together.

steps.title: The coverings have different histories
steps.stepSummary: The גְּמָרָא distinguishes a covering designated for תְּפִילִּין from one that was not.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not difficult: one case involves a covering designated for תפילין, and the other involves one that was not designated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גְּמָרָא answers that the teachings describe different coverings. It is setting up the next statement, which explains how designation and actual use affect the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The prohibition is assigned to the designated covering, and the permission to the undesignated one. The next step makes this distinction more precise.

keyTerms.meaning: this is not difficult; the apparent conflict can be resolved
that he did not designate it

phrases.english: This is not difficult: This case is where he designated it.
That case is where he did not designate it.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא, הָא דְּאַזְמְנֵיהּ.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the apparent conflict by assigning the two rulings to different cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes whether the covering was designated for תְּפִילִּין.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both teachings address the same kind of covering.
steps.terutzMaskana: The coverings differ in whether they were designated for תְּפִילִּין.

steps.title: A designated cloth that was used has a restriction
steps.stepSummary: רַב חִסְדָּא says the cloth cannot hold money when it was both designated for תְּפִילִּין and used for them.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב חסדא said: If a cloth was designated for bundling תפילין and תפילין were bundled in it, one may not bundle coins in it. If it was designated but not used, or used but not designated, one may bundle money in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גְּמָרָא brings רַב חִסְדָּא’s rule to explain the distinction. His rule adds an important detail: for him, designation and actual use must both occur before money is forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Designation alone does not forbid money according to רַב חִסְדָּא. Actual use alone does not forbid it either. The restriction applies only when the cloth has both.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: הַאי סוּדָרָא דִתְפִילִּין
phrases.english: For Rav Ḥisda said: This cloth for phylacteries,
which he designated for bundling phylacteries in it—

phrases.aramaic: צָר בֵּיהּ תְּפִילִּין — אָסוּר לְמֵיצַר בֵּיהּ פְּשִׁיטֵי,
phrases.english: if he bundled phylacteries in it, it is forbidden to bundle coins in it;
if he designated it but did not bundle them in it,
or bundled them in it but did not designate it—
it is permitted to bundle money in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: הַאי סוּדָרָא דִתְפִילִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports and sharpens the distinction about a designated covering.
steps.raayaObject: The distinction between coverings used for תְּפִילִּין.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רַב חִסְדָּא’s rule about designation together with actual use.

steps.title: Designation alone matters according to אביי
steps.stepSummary: For אַבָּיֵי, designation by itself is enough to forbid putting money in the cloth; use without designation is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to אביי, who says designation is significant: If he designated the cloth, even without bundling תפילין in it, the restriction applies. If he bundled them in it, it is forbidden when he designated it, but not when he did not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גְּמָרָא now states how אַבָּיֵי would apply the rule. Unlike רַב חִסְדָּא, he treats designation alone as sufficient.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For אַבָּיֵי, a designated cloth may not hold money even before it has held תְּפִילִּין. If it held תְּפִילִּין without being designated, that use alone does not create the restriction.

phrases.english: And according to Abaye, who said designation is significant:

phrases.aramaic: אַזְמְנֵיהּ אַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא צָר בֵּיהּ.
phrases.english: if he designated it, even though he did not bundle them in it.
If he bundled them in it, then if he designated it, it is forbidden;
if he did not designate it, it is not.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְאַבָּיֵי דְּאָמַר הַזְמָנָה מִילְּתָא הִיא:
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives אַבָּיֵי’s different threshold for when the same restriction begins.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For אַבָּיֵי, designation forbids putting money in the cloth even without prior use; use without designation does not.

steps.title: May תפילין be placed under one’s head?
steps.stepSummary: רַב יוֹסֵף בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב נְחוּנְיָא asks רַב יְהוּדָה about placing תְּפִילִּין under the head while sleeping, distinguishing this from placing them under the feet.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף son of רב נחוניא asked רב יהודה: May a person place his תפילין under his head? I am not asking about under his feet, because that treats them disrespectfully. My question is specifically about under his head.
steps.whatsHappening: The גְּמָרָא moves to a new question about where to place תְּפִילִּין during sleep. The questioner rules out placement under the feet and asks only about placement under the head.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the feet is already understood to be disrespectful. Under the head may be different, so the questioner asks for a ruling on that case.

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב יוֹסֵף בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב נְחוּנְיָא מֵרַב יְהוּדָה:
phrases.english: Rav Yosef, son of Rav Neḥunya, asked Rav Yehuda:

phrases.aramaic: מַהוּ שֶׁיַּנִּיחַ אָדָם תְּפִילָּיו תַּחַת מְרַאֲשׁוֹתָיו?
phrases.english: May a person place his phylacteries under his head?

phrases.aramaic: תַּחַת מַרְגְּלוֹתָיו לָא קָא מִיבַּעְיָא לִי,
phrases.english: About placing them under his feet, I have no question,
because that treats them disrespectfully.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי קָא מִיבַּעְיָא לִי, תַּחַת מְרַאֲשׁוֹתָיו מַאי?
phrases.english: What I am asking is: What about under his head?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב יוֹסֵף בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב נְחוּנְיָא מֵרַב יְהוּדָה:
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the question of storing money with תְּפִילִּין and opens a question about their placement during sleep.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether placing תְּפִילִּין under one’s head is permitted.

steps.title: Placing them under the head is permitted
steps.stepSummary: רַב יְהוּדָה reports שְׁמוּאֵל’s permission, even when the man’s wife is with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He answered him: שמואל said that it is permitted, even if his wife is with him.
steps.whatsHappening: רַב יְהוּדָה answers the specific question about placement under the head. He reports that שְׁמוּאֵל permits it even when the man’s wife is with him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer permits the case the questioner was unsure about. It does not change his earlier point that placing תְּפִילִּין under the feet is disrespectful.
steps.whatToRemember: The permission answers the question about under the head, not under the feet.

phrases.english: He said to him: Shmuel said as follows:
It is permitted, even if his wife is with him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָכִי אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question about placing תְּפִילִּין under the head.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: שְׁמוּאֵל permits placing תְּפִילִּין under the head, even when the man’s wife is with him.

steps.title: A teaching challenges the permission when his wife is present
steps.stepSummary: A בָּרַיְיתָא permits תְּפִילִּין under the head but forbids it when the man’s wife is with him, unless there is a place three handbreadths higher or lower.
steps.simpleTranslation: An objection: A person may not put his תְּפִילִּין under his feet, because that treats them disrespectfully. He may put them under his head, but not if his wife is with him. A place three handbreadths higher or lower is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גְּמָרָא brings a בָּרַיְיתָא to challenge שְׁמוּאֵל’s permission from the previous step. It spells out both the restriction and an exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The בָּרַיְיתָא agrees that putting תְּפִילִּין under the head can be allowed. The conflict is the case where the man’s wife is with him: שְׁמוּאֵל permits it, while this בָּרַיְיתָא forbids it unless the תְּפִילִּין are in a sufficiently higher or lower place.

phrases.english: They object: A person may not place his phylacteries
under the area by his feet, because he treats them
in a disrespectful way; but he may place them
under the area by his head.
And if his wife was with him, it is prohibited.
If there was a place three handbreadths higher
or three handbreadths lower, it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: לָא יַנִּיחַ אָדָם תְּפִילָּיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שְׁמוּאֵל’s permission in the case where the man’s wife is with him.
steps.kashyaTarget: שְׁמוּאֵל’s permission to place תְּפִילִּין under the head even when the wife is present.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The בָּרַיְיתָא explicitly prohibits that same case, apart from its stated higher-or-lower-place exception.

steps.title: The challenge to שמואל is accepted
steps.stepSummary: The גְּמָרָא calls the בָּרַיְיתָא a conclusive refutation of שְׁמוּאֵל.
steps.simpleTranslation: A conclusive refutation of שמואל—indeed, a conclusive refutation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גְּמָרָא accepts the challenge to שְׁמוּאֵל’s statement. This closes the immediate objection, before רָבָא makes a new move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The repeated word says that the conflict with the בָּרַיְיתָא stands. It does not yet tell us what the final practical ruling will be.

keyTerms.meaning: Of שמואל; identifies whose statement is refuted.
A refutation specifically of שמואל’s statement.

phrases.english: A conclusive refutation of Shmuel; a conclusive refutation.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּיוּבְתָּא דִשְׁמוּאֵל, תְּיוּבְתָּא.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Confirms that the בָּרַיְיתָא successfully challenges שְׁמוּאֵל’s statement.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The objection to שְׁמוּאֵל stands; the practical ruling has not yet been settled.

steps.title: רבא nevertheless rules like שמואל
steps.stepSummary: רָבָא acknowledges the refutation but says the הֲלָכָה follows שְׁמוּאֵל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Although a conclusive refutation of שמואל was taught, the law follows him.
steps.whatsHappening: רָבָא gives a practical ruling despite the accepted challenge. The גְּמָרָא is now moving from whether שְׁמוּאֵל was refuted to why his ruling is still followed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רָבָא does not deny what the בָּרַיְיתָא says. He states that, even so, the הֲלָכָה in this matter is like שְׁמוּאֵל.

phrases.english: Rava said: Even though
a conclusive refutation of Shmuel was taught,
the law follows him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: אַף עַל גַּב דְּתַנְיָא תְּיוּבְתָּא דִשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the refutation but gives a ruling that follows the refuted statement.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הֲלָכָה follows שְׁמוּאֵל in this matter despite the בָּרַיְיתָא’s challenge.

steps.title: The גמרא asks why רבא follows שמואל
steps.stepSummary: The גְּמָרָא asks for the reason behind רָבָא’s ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גְּמָרָא asks why רָבָא rules like שְׁמוּאֵל despite the refutation. This question sets up an explanation in the next part of the sugya.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question does not erase the challenge or supply an answer. It asks what supports the practical ruling after that challenge was accepted.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Requests a reason for רָבָא’s ruling after the accepted refutation.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the הֲלָכָה follows שְׁמוּאֵל despite the בָּרַיְיתָא’s conclusive challenge.
